content:
# Disagreement Log — 1 Maccabees Chapter 1

**Date:** 2026-03-17
**Translators:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA

---

## Summary
Total disagreements: 41

---

## Disagreement Entries

**1MA 1:1 — Structure of opening sentence**
- EMET: Preserves the LXX's extended "And it came to pass after..." structure, echoing Samuel/Kings
- LOGOS: Modernizes to a subordinate clause without "And it came to pass"
- PNEUMA: Opens with "This is what happened after..." — narrative frame
- RULING: SOPHIA adopts LOGOS structure with EMET's opening framing retained implicitly

**1MA 1:3 — "the earth fell silent before him"**
- EMET: "the earth fell silent before him"
- LOGOS: "The earth grew quiet before him"
- PNEUMA: "The world went silent before him"
- RULING: "The earth fell silent before him" — "fell silent" is more abrupt and appropriate to the military context

**1MA 1:4 — "provinces and nations and dominions" vs. "provinces, nations, and princes"**
- EMET: "lands and nations and dominions"
- LOGOS/PNEUMA: "provinces and nations and rulers/princes"
- RULING: "provinces and nations and rulers" — the Greek *dynastas* means those who hold power, not abstract dominions

**1MA 1:5 — "fell upon his bed"**
- EMET: "fell upon his bed"
- LOGOS: "fell ill"
- PNEUMA: "took to his bed"
- RULING: "fell upon his bed" — the idiom is biblical and should be preserved; it echoes the language of 1 Kings

**1MA 1:10 — "sinful root" vs. "sinful offshoot"**
- EMET: "sinful root"
- LOGOS/PNEUMA: "sinful offshoot"
- RULING: "sinful root" — the Greek *rhiza* is "root," the source of evil, not a branch from it; the metaphor points to corrupted origin

**1MA 1:11 — "lawless men" introduction**
- EMET/LOGOS: "lawless men went out from Israel"
- PNEUMA: "certain lawless men rose up in Israel"
- RULING: "certain lawless men went out from Israel" — "went out" reflects the Greek *exelthon* and the communal break implied

**1MA 1:11 — "many evils have found us"**
- EMET: "many evils have found us"
- LOGOS: "we have encountered much trouble"
- PNEUMA: "nothing but trouble has found us"
- RULING: "many evils have found us" — literal and retains the passive construction of evil "finding" them rather than them finding evil

**1MA 1:14 — "gymnasium"**
- All agree: "gymnasium" preserved as Greek loanword. No disagreement.

**1MA 1:15 — "made themselves foreskins" vs. "had themselves uncircumcised" vs. "reversed their circumcisions"**
- EMET: "made themselves foreskins"
- LOGOS: "had themselves uncircumcised"
- PNEUMA: "reversed their circumcisions"
- RULING: "had themselves uncircumcised" — EMET is overly literal to the point of obscurity; LOGOS conveys the surgical reality (epispasm) while maintaining dignity

**1MA 1:16 — "purposed to reign" vs. "determined to become king"**
- EMET: "purposed to reign over Egypt"
- LOGOS/PNEUMA: "determined to become king / set his sights on Egypt"
- RULING: "determined to reign over Egypt"

**1MA 1:17 — Order of military forces**
- Minor word-order variations between translators. No substantive disagreement.

**1MA 1:20 — "went up against Israel" vs. "marched against Israel"**
- EMET: "went up against Israel"
- LOGOS/PNEUMA: "marched against / advanced against"
- RULING: "advanced against Israel" — "went up" is idiomatic Hebrew preserved in the Greek; acceptable in formal but "advanced" is clearer

**1MA 1:21 — "lampstand of light" vs. "lampstand for the light"**
- EMET: "lampstand of light"
- LOGOS: "lampstand for the light"
- PNEUMA: "lampstand with all its fittings" (expands)
- RULING: "lampstand for the light" — the genitive indicates purpose

**1MA 1:22 — "table of the showbread" vs. "table of the bread of the Presence"**
- EMET: "table of the showbread"
- LOGOS/PNEUMA: "table of the bread of the Presence"
- RULING: "table of the bread of the Presence" — modern standard; "showbread" is archaic

**1MA 1:22 — "golden decoration on the face of the temple"**
- EMET: "golden decoration on the face of the temple"
- LOGOS: "golden decoration on the facade of the temple"
- PNEUMA: "golden ornamentation from the face of the temple"
- RULING: "golden decoration from the facade of the temple"

**1MA 1:24 — "having made a great slaughter" vs. "having shed much blood"**
- EMET: "having made a great slaughter"
- LOGOS: "He had shed much blood"
- PNEUMA: "leaving massacre in his wake"
- RULING: "He had shed much blood" — clean and direct

**1MA 1:25 — "in every place" vs. "in every corner of the land"**
- EMET/LOGOS: "in every place"
- PNEUMA: "in every corner of the land"
- RULING: "in every place" — the Greek *kata topon* is general; PNEUMA adds "land" without warrant

**1MA 1:26 — "beauty of the women was altered"**
- EMET/LOGOS: "beauty of the women was altered"
- PNEUMA: "faces of the women changed color"
- RULING: "beauty of the women was altered" — closer to the Greek *emetablethen*

**1MA 1:27 — "she who sat in the bridal chamber"**
- All translators agree on this rendering. No substantive disagreement.

**1MA 1:29 — "chief tribute-collector" vs. "chief collector of tribute" vs. "senior tax official"**
- EMET: "chief tribute-collector"
- LOGOS: "chief collector of tribute"
- PNEUMA: "senior tax official"
- RULING: "chief collector of tribute" — preserves the technical character without being awkward

**1MA 1:30 — "words of peace in deceit"**
- EMET: "words of peace in deceit"
- LOGOS: "peaceful words, but in deceit"
- PNEUMA: "in friendly terms — a lie they believed"
- RULING: "words of peace, but in deceit" — the adversative conjunction is important

**1MA 1:33 — "city of David"**
- All agree: "city of David" = the Akra / Zion citadel. No disagreement.

**1MA 1:35 — "great snare" vs. "grave danger"**
- EMET: "great snare"
- LOGOS: "grave danger"
- PNEUMA: "trap set in the heart of the city"
- RULING: "grave danger" — the Greek *skandalon* here means a dangerous stumbling block, not a hunting trap

**1MA 1:36 — "lying-in-wait" vs. "ambush"**
- EMET: "lying-in-wait"
- LOGOS/PNEUMA: "ambush"
- RULING: "ambush" — more natural English

**1MA 1:36 — "evil adversary" vs. "constant evil adversary"**
- EMET: "evil adversary continually"
- LOGOS: "constant evil adversary"
- PNEUMA: "festering wound in Israel's side"
- RULING: "constant evil adversary to Israel" — PNEUMA's metaphor, though vivid, departs from the text

**1MA 1:38 — "dwelling of strangers" vs. "habitation for strangers"**
- Minor variation. LOGOS: "habitation for strangers." EMET: "dwelling of strangers." No substantive difference.
- RULING: "habitation for strangers" — slightly elevated register suits the lament passage

**1MA 1:39 — "sabbaths into reproach" vs. "sabbaths to shame"**
- EMET: "sabbaths into reproach"
- LOGOS: "sabbaths to shame"
- PNEUMA: "sabbaths turned to mockery"
- RULING: "sabbaths to disgrace" — a middle ground; "reproach" is archaic, "mockery" adds a nuance not in the Greek

**1MA 1:40 — "high estate" vs. "exaltation" vs. "high dignity"**
- EMET: "exaltation was turned into mourning"
- LOGOS: "high estate was turned into grief"
- PNEUMA: "exaltation was swallowed by grief"
- RULING: "her high dignity was turned into grief" — "high dignity" captures *hupsos* well

**1MA 1:41-42 — Structure of the universalizing decree**
- EMET: Renders as two short sentences
- LOGOS/PNEUMA: Integrate into one flowing sentence
- RULING: Two sentences retained — the abruptness mirrors the original's staccato royal decree style

**1MA 1:43 — "consented to his worship" vs. "accepted his religion willingly"**
- EMET: "consented to his worship"
- LOGOS: "willingly accepted his religion"
- PNEUMA: "went along"
- RULING: "accepted his religion willingly" — captures the voluntary apostasy

**1MA 1:46 — "sacred precincts and shrines" vs. "sacred groves and idolatrous shrines"**
- EMET: "sacred precincts and shrines for idols"
- LOGOS: "sacred groves and idolatrous shrines"
- PNEUMA: "pagan altars, sacred groves, idol shrines"
- RULING: "sacred precincts and shrines for idols" — *temene* means demarcated sacred precincts, not necessarily tree groves

**1MA 1:47 — "unclean animals"**
- All agree. No disagreement on the list of prohibited items.

**1MA 1:49 — "forget the Torah" vs. "abandon all its ordinances"**
- EMET/LOGOS: "forget the Torah and change all the ordinances"
- PNEUMA: "forget the Torah and overturn every ordinance"
- RULING: "forget the Torah and abandon all its ordinances" — "abandon" reflects *exaleiphein* (to wipe out)

**1MA 1:50 — "he would die" vs. "would die"**
- Minor stylistic difference. No substantive disagreement.

**1MA 1:51 — "overseers" vs. "inspectors" vs. "enforcers"**
- EMET: "overseers"
- LOGOS: "inspectors"
- PNEUMA: "enforcers"
- RULING: "overseers" — the Greek *episkopoi* is "overseers"; PNEUMA's "enforcers" adds punitive nuance not explicit in the text

**1MA 1:54 — "desolating abomination"**
- All agree: "desolating abomination." This is the standard rendering of *bdelugma eremoseos* echoing Daniel 11:31.

**1MA 1:57 — "scroll of the covenant"**
- All agree: "scroll of the covenant." No disagreement.

**1MA 1:58 — "In their might" vs. "Month after month"**
- EMET: "In their might they acted against Israel"
- LOGOS/PNEUMA: "Month after month" (interpreting *kata mena* as temporal)
- RULING: "Month after month" — *kata mena* most naturally reads as temporal; EMET's reading lacks support

**1MA 1:60-61 — Syntax of the execution decree**
- EMET/LOGOS: "put to death according to the decree"
- PNEUMA: "were executed"
- RULING: LOGOS structure retained with clearer passive construction

**1MA 1:62 — "stood firm and were strengthened in themselves"**
- EMET: "stood firm and were strengthened in themselves"
- LOGOS/PNEUMA: "stood firm" / "held firm" (simplified)
- RULING: "stood firm, resolving in their hearts" — the self-deliberative aspect (*en heautois*) is important and should be retained

**1MA 1:63 — "chose to die rather than to be defiled"**
- All three translators agree on this rendering. No disagreement.

**1MA 1:64 — "very great wrath"**
- EMET: "very great wrath came upon Israel"
- LOGOS: "very great wrath fell upon Israel"
- PNEUMA: "Terrible wrath came crashing down"
- RULING: "very great wrath came upon Israel" — the understated closing mirrors the biblical historical style the author employs throughout
